claims.label: Theorem 4.4
claims.statement_original:
Assuming (N), the following are equivalent.
(a) There exists a unique maximum element $\mu$ in convex order in $\mathcal M_\gamma$, i.e., $\mu\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}\gamma$ and for each $
u$ supported on $\mathcal I^+$ with $
u\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}\gamma$, it holds that $
u\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}\mu$.
(b) The class of measures $\{\mu_x\}_{x\ge0}$ from Proposition 4.3 is monotone (in the usual order), i.e., for all $x\le y$, $\mu_x\le\mu_y$.

claims.label: Theorem 4.7
claims.statement_original: Assume (N), (JA), (AC). Suppose that there exists a convex set $\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ such that $\gamma(\partial\Gamma)=1$. Then there exists a unique maximum element $\mu$ in convex order in $\mathcal M_\gamma$. Moreover, $\mu$ is the unique probability measure on the $\mathcal I_2^+$ with $\mu([0,x]^2)=\mu_x(\mathbb R^2)$, where $\mu_x$ was given in Proposition 4.3 applied with $L=2$. In particular, there exist distinct measures $F,G\in\Pi(\mathbb R)$ such that $(dF/dG,dF/dG)|_G=\mu$, attaining the maximum in (7).

claims.label: Theorem 4.9
claims.statement_original:
Suppose that $\mathcal X$ is an Euclidean space and $P_1,\ldots,P_L$ are distinct probability measures on $\mathcal X$. If $Q\in\Pi(\mathcal X)$ satisfies $Q
otin\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots,P_L\}$, then there exists $k\ge1$ such that $Q^k
otin\operatorname{Span}\mathcal P^k$ (and in particular $Q^k
otin\operatorname{Conv}\mathcal P^k$). Moreover, if we also assume that $Q$ satisfies (AC) and that $P_1,\ldots,P_L$ are linearly independent, then either $Q
otin\operatorname{Span}\mathcal P$ or $Q^2
otin\operatorname{Span}\mathcal P^2$ (or both); in particular, either $Q
otin\operatorname{Conv}\mathcal P$ or $Q^2
otin\operatorname{Conv}\mathcal P^2$ (or both).

claims.label: Theorem 5.3
claims.statement_original: Assume (JA) and (AC). For any $s$, we have $\mu^{(s)}\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}\mu^{(s+1)}$, and if $\mu^{(s)}\ne\mu^{(s+1)}$, then the inequality is strict, meaning that the above SHINE construction makes progress at each step. Further, assuming (N), it produces a sequence of measures that converges almost surely to a maximal element $\mu$ in convex order in $\mathcal M_\gamma$. In this case, if there exists a maximum element $\mu_0$, then the output of our SHINE construction converges to $\mu_0$.

claims.label: Theorem 5.5
claims.statement_original:
Assume the same conditions as in Theorem 5.3. Suppose that there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that
\[
\mathbb E^Q\left[\left(\frac{dP_j}{dQ}\right)^{2+\varepsilon}\right]<\infty,\quad\text{for some }j,
\]
(14)
and
\[
\mathbb E^Q\left[\left(\frac{dP_{j'}}{dQ}\right)^{-2}\right]<\infty,\quad\text{for some }j'.
\]
(15)
Consider the e-power $\mathrm{EP}_k:=\mathbb E^Q[-\log X_k]$ where $\{X_k\}$ is the SHINE martingale. Then there exist $r\in(0,1)$ and $C>0$ such that
\[
\mathrm{EP}_\infty-\mathrm{EP}_k\le Cr^k,
\]
where $\mathrm{EP}_\infty=\mathbb E[-\log X_\infty]$ and $X_k\to X_\infty$ a.s.

Theorem 6.2
Theorem 6.7
claims.statement_original: Assume that there exists a common reference measure $R\in\Pi(\mathcal X)$ such that $P\ll R$ for $P\in\mathcal P$ and $Q\ll R$ for $Q\in\mathcal Q$. There exists an exact bounded e-variable $X$ for $\mathcal P$ against $\mathcal Q$ satisfying $\inf_{Q\in\mathcal Q}\mathbb E^Q[\log X]>0$ if and only if $0\notin\overline{\overline{\operatorname{Span}}\mathcal P+\overline{\operatorname{Conv}}\mathcal Q}$, where the closure is taken with respect to the total variation distance. If $\mathcal Q$ is tight, then we have the further equivalence to $\overline{\operatorname{Span}}\mathcal P\cap\overline{\operatorname{Conv}}\mathcal Q=\varnothing$.
